content: Redness in the eye occurs due to the swelling or dilation of blood vessels, which makes the surface of the eye appear red or bloodshot. There are numerous potential causes for red eyes, ranging from benign conditions to medical emergencies. The severity of redness is often less concerning than the presence of associated symptoms such as eye pain or visual disturbances. The redness is caused by the swelling of blood vessels on the sclera, the white part of the eye. Allergies, infections, or injuries can also contribute. A common cause of red eyes is straining or coughing, which may lead to a bright red, dense bloody spot on the sclera, known as a subconjunctival hemorrhage. While this may appear alarming, it is generally harmless and resolves on its own within one to two weeks. Eye infections or inflammation can also lead to redness, often accompanied by symptoms such as itching, discharge, pain, or vision problems. Specific conditions include: Blepharitis: Inflammation of the eyelid margin, particularly around the eyelashes. Conjunctivitis: Inflammation or infection of the conjunctiva, the tissue lining the eyelids and covering the sclera, commonly referred to as pink eye. Corneal ulcers: Open sores on the cornea, typically caused by bacterial or viral infections. Uveitis: Inflammation of the uvea, which includes the iris, ciliary body, and choroid. When only the iris is inflamed, it is termed iritis. Other potential causes of red eyes include: Colds or allergies. This is a medical emergency, though most cases of glaucoma develop gradually over time. Corneal abrasions, which may result from sand, dust, or improper contact lens use. During a physical examination, your doctor will assess your eyes and inquire about your medical history. Questions may include: Are one or both eyes affected? If only one, which eye? What part of the eye is red—just the sclera or another area? Did the redness develop suddenly or gradually? Have you experienced eye redness in the past? Are you experiencing eye pain, and does it worsen with eye movement? Are there additional symptoms such as discharge, burning, itching, nausea, vomiting, or headache? You should seek immediate medical attention if: The redness follows a penetrating eye injury. You experience a headache along with blurred vision or confusion. You see halos around lights. You have nausea and vomiting. Contact your healthcare provider if: The redness persists for more than one to two days. You experience eye pain or changes in vision. You are taking blood-thinning medications like warfarin. You suspect a foreign object is in your eye. You are highly sensitive to light. You notice yellow or green discharge from one or both eyes. For mild cases caused by fatigue or eyestrain, resting your eyes may suffice, and no specific treatment is necessary. However, if you experience pain or vision problems, consult a healthcare professional. Treatment may involve rinsing the eyes with saline solution, removing foreign objects, or using prescribed eye drops.
